promptText:
ROLE: Act as a mathematics teacher who designs open-ended investigations that build reasoning and pattern-spotting.

CONTEXT: I teach [CLASS/GRADE] under [BOARD or EXAM e.g. CBSE / ICSE / State Board]. I want one INVESTIGATION TASK on [TOPIC or STARTING IDEA e.g. number patterns / areas of shapes on a grid / properties of digits]. Students should explore, find a pattern, make a conjecture, and justify it. It should suit [TIME e.g. one or two periods].

YOUR TASK:
1. Pose one intriguing starting question that invites exploration.
2. Give a few warm-up cases students can compute to get going.
3. Provide a ladder of 3 graded hints (gentle to strong) that guide without spoiling.
4. State the expected pattern, conjecture and a short justification (for the teacher only).
5. Suggest 2 extension questions for fast finishers.
6. Provide a rubric (15 marks) that rewards reasoning, not just the final answer.

INPUT: Here is my topic or starting idea: [PASTE TOPIC HERE]. If blank, choose a rich, age-appropriate investigation for the class and board above.

HOW TO WORK IT OUT: Work the investigation through internally to be sure a real pattern exists. VERIFY the pattern with at least three worked cases and a short proof or clear argument; show these checks in the teacher section. Never claim a pattern you have not verified. Keep all maths legible in clean plain text or simple LaTeX.

OUTPUT FORMAT (use these exact headings in this order):
1. INVESTIGATION TITLE
2. THE STARTING QUESTION (student-facing)
3. WARM-UP CASES (for students to try)
4. HINT LADDER (Hint 1 / Hint 2 / Hint 3)
5. EXPECTED FINDINGS - TEACHER ONLY (pattern + conjecture + justification + the three verification cases)
6. EXTENSIONS
7. RUBRIC (15 marks, criteria focused on reasoning)

RULES: Keep the student-facing part free of spoilers. Be precise. Short, plain sentences.

Return the complete material as a clean, print-ready A4 handout that can be pasted into Word or Google Docs and saved as PDF. Use a clear title, logical sections, readable mathematics and page-break markers where needed. Keep student material separate from the answer key or teacher notes.

title: Cross-Curricular Project (Maths + Another Subject)
whatYouGet: A project linking maths to science, art, history or geography, with combined rubric.
howToUse: Pick the maths topic and the partner subject, paste it in, and share the joint project brief.
effectiveUsage: 1. Fill in maths topic, partner subject, class.
2. Paste the prompt into any AI chat.
3. Check how the two subjects link.
4. Copy the brief into a document.
5. Grade with the combined rubric.
commonFix: If the link feels forced, reply: "Make the connection between maths and the other subject more genuine and central, and re-verify any calculations."
promptText:
ROLE: Act as a maths teacher who designs cross-curricular projects that link mathematics meaningfully to another subject.

CONTEXT: I teach [CLASS/GRADE] under [BOARD e.g. CBSE / ICSE / State Board]. I want a CROSS-CURRICULAR PROJECT linking the maths topic [MATHS TOPIC e.g. ratios / geometry / data] with the subject [OTHER SUBJECT e.g. Science / Art / History / Geography / Music]. The maths must be central, not decoration.

YOUR TASK:
1. State the genuine link between the maths topic and the other subject.
2. Give a student-facing project goal and concrete deliverable.
3. Provide numbered steps showing exactly where the maths is used.
4. Include one worked example demonstrating the maths in this context.
5. Provide a combined rubric (20 marks) covering both the maths and the other-subject content.
6. Add 2 differentiation ideas.

INPUT: Here is my maths topic and the partner subject: [PASTE MATHS TOPIC AND OTHER SUBJECT HERE]. If blank, choose a strong pairing for the class and board above.

HOW TO WORK IT OUT: Plan internally and ensure the maths does real work in the project. VERIFY any calculation two ways and show both checks. Keep facts from the other subject accurate; if unsure of a fact, say so rather than inventing it. Never invent formulas. Keep all maths legible in clean plain text or simple LaTeX.

OUTPUT FORMAT (use these exact headings in this order):
1. PROJECT TITLE
2. THE MATHS-AND-[SUBJECT] LINK
3. PROJECT GOAL AND DELIVERABLE
4. STUDENT STEPS (numbered; mark where the maths is used)
5. WORKED EXAMPLE WITH TWO CHECKS
6. COMBINED RUBRIC (20 marks; show which marks are maths and which are the other subject)
7. DIFFERENTIATION (2 ideas)
8. TEACHER TIPS

RULES: The maths must be essential. Be specific and accurate. Short, plain sentences.

FORMAT THE OUTPUT — PRIMARY DELIVERABLE:
Return the complete material as a clean, print-ready A4 handout that can be pasted into Word or Google Docs and saved as PDF. Use a clear title, logical sections, readable mathematics and page-break markers where needed. Keep student material separate from the answer key or teacher notes.


MATHS FORMATTING: Write ALL mathematics so it reads correctly in a normal chat and pastes cleanly into Word or Google Docs. Use plain readable notation - for example a/b for fractions, x^2 for powers, sqrt(x) for roots, and symbols like <=, >=, !=, +-, pi, theta, integral and sum. Do NOT output raw LaTeX or code such as \frac{}{}, \sqrt{}, x^{2}, $...$ or \( ... \) - these appear as broken symbols to a teacher in a free chat.

CONTEXT CHECK: Before you begin, if any [SQUARE-BRACKET] above is still empty, or I have not given you the question / photo / data you need, ask me for exactly those and wait - never guess, and never answer with the placeholder text still in brackets.

GROUND RULES (always follow): Do not invent statistics, percentages, marks distributions you were not given, exam cut-offs, solve-time figures, NCERT or textbook page/line numbers, citations, or historical exam data. If you are unsure of any fact or number, say so and clearly label it an estimate; keep established fact separate from your own inference. Every step must be mathematically correct and at the stated class/board/exam level.

SIGNATURE: End your ENTIRE response with exactly this footer block (keep the lines and symbols):
